#1 This is more for the sake of amusement than anything else: perhaps the softest imaginable proof of the chain rule for formal power series.

Working over a commutative ring AAA, the statement is that if q,p∈A[[x]]q, p \in A[ [x] ]q,p∈A[[x]] are power series, with 000 the constant coefficient of ppp, then (q∘p)′(x)=q′(p(x))p′(x)(q \circ p)'(x) = q'(p(x))p'(x)(q∘p)′(x)=q′(p(x))p′(x) under the usual definitions.

Let D=A[y]/(y2)D = A[y]/(y^2)D=A[y]/(y2) be the representing object for derivations. Let δ:A[[x]]→A[[x]]⊗AD≅A[[x]][y]/(y2)\delta: A[ [x] ] \to A[ [x] ] \otimes_A D \cong A[ [x] ][y]/(y^2)δ:A[[x]]→A[[x]]⊗A​D≅A[[x]][y]/(y2) be the unique topological AAA-algebra map (under the (x)(x)(x)-adic topologies) that sends xxx to x+yx + yx+y. (If it helps, think δ(q)=q(x+y)\delta(q) = q(x + y)δ(q)=q(x+y).) For p∈A[[x]]p \in A[ [x] ]p∈A[[x]], define p′p'p′ via the equation δ(p)=p(x)+p′(x)y\delta(p) = p(x) + p'(x)yδ(p)=p(x)+p′(x)y.

Let π:A[[x]]⊗AD→A[[x]]⊗AD\pi: A[ [x] ] \otimes_A D \to A[ [x] ] \otimes_A Dπ:A[[x]]⊗A​D→A[[x]]⊗A​D be the unique topological algebra map taking xxx to p(x)p(x)p(x) and yyy to p′(x)yp'(x)yp′(x)y. Let −∘p:A[[x]]→A[[x]]- \circ p: A[ [x] ] \to A[ [x] ]−∘p:A[[x]]→A[[x]] denote the unique topological algebra map that takes xxx to ppp. Then the diagram

A[[x]]→δA[[x]]⊗AD−∘p↓↓πA[[x]]→δA[[x]]⊗AD\begin{matrix} A[ [x] ] & \stackrel{\delta}{\to} & A[ [x] ] \otimes_A D \\ \mathllap{- \circ p} \downarrow & & \downarrow \mathrlap{\pi} \\ A[ [x] ] & \underset{\delta}{\to} & A[ [x] ] \otimes_A D \end{matrix}A[[x]]−∘p↓A[[x]]​→δδ→​​A[[x]]⊗A​D↓πA[[x]]⊗A​D​

commutes in the category of topological algebras, since the two legs agree when evaluated at the generator xxx. But then, evaluating each leg at a power series q∈A[[x]]q \in A [ [x]]q∈A[[x]], we have

[δ(−∘p)](q)=δ(q∘p)=(q∘p)(x)+(q∘p)′(x)y[\delta(- \circ p)](q) = \delta(q \circ p) = (q \circ p)(x) + (q \circ p)'(x)y[δ(−∘p)](q)=δ(q∘p)=(q∘p)(x)+(q∘p)′(x)y

and

[πδ](q)=π(δ(q))=π(q(x)+q′(x)y)=q(p(x))+q′(p(x))(p′(x)y)[\pi \delta](q) = \pi(\delta(q)) = \pi(q(x) + q'(x)y) = q(p(x)) + q'(p(x))(p'(x)y)[πδ](q)=π(δ(q))=π(q(x)+q′(x)y)=q(p(x))+q′(p(x))(p′(x)y)

whence the coefficients of yyy agree: (q∘p)′(x)=q′(p(x))p′(x)(q \circ p)'(x) = q'(p(x))p'(x)(q∘p)′(x)=q′(p(x))p′(x).
subject: soft proof of the chain rule

content:
#2 Well, I’ll admit it’s a little silly, almost parodic in the manner of Mathematics Made Difficult. A halfway normal proof might start the same way but then observe that in the ring with square-nilpotent yyy we have

(p(x)+p′(x)y)n=p(x)+np(x)n−1p′(x)y\left(p(x) + p'(x)y\right)^n = p(x) + n p(x)^{n-1} p'(x)y(p(x)+p′(x)y)n=p(x)+np(x)n−1p′(x)y

say by the binomial theorem, or by an inductive argument. This gives the chain rule (q∘p)′(x)=q′(p(x))⋅p′(x)(q \circ p)'(x) = q'(p(x)) \cdot p'(x)(q∘p)′(x)=q′(p(x))⋅p′(x) at least for q(x)=xnq(x) = x^nq(x)=xn. Then extend to all power series q(x)=∑n≥0anxnq(x) = \sum_{n \geq 0} a_n x^nq(x)=∑n≥0​an​xn by linearity, continuity, etc. Of course that’s just one approach; there are others (such as ‘meta’ approaches that observe that the usual analysis proof implies the result in formal algebra).

Any of those could be easier to follow than what I produced above. So what’s the point? Nothing, really, except that it amused me that one could prove the statement with virtually zero calculation (like the binomial theorem) anywhere – just by sticking to pure concepts and using the universal property of A[[x]]A[ [x] ]A[[x]].
subject: soft proof of the chain rule

content:
#4 Thanks! I just meant that with that definition of p′p'p′, we prove the chain rule with a minimum of calculation. Other properties might require more calculation.

Of course, the definition is just the algebraic analogue of something familiar from SDG: if p:R→Rp: R \to Rp:R→R is a function on the line and DDD denotes the walking tangent vector, then under the Kock-Lawvere axiom which asserts an isomorphism R×R≅RDR \times R \cong R^DR×R≅RD we may form a composite

R→ΔR×R≅RD→pDRD≅R×RR \stackrel{\Delta}{\to} R \times R \cong R^D \stackrel{p^D}{\to} R^D \cong R \times RR→ΔR×R≅RD→pDRD≅R×R

which is just ⟨p,p′⟩:R→R×R\langle p, p' \rangle: R \to R \times R⟨p,p′⟩:R→R×R. (It’s a little easy here to get turned around with algebro-geometric duality, but I believe it works as advertised.) Even with all these hints, though, plus the fact that the chain rule is trying to express the functoriality of the tangent bundle vector (−)D(-)^D(−)D, it still took me some time to massage it into the form above.
subject: soft proof of the chain rule

content: #5 Ah, I didn’t realise that this definition of p′p'p′ was one of the novel aspects, even if inspired by SDG. Then the observation is nicer still!

content:
#8 Giving a reference is a slight embarrassment of riches problem. (If Urs is reading this, he might know a canonical reference right away.) Let me show the definition gives the correct answer in the mother of all contexts which is that of real-valued C∞C^\inftyC∞ functions, rather than power series with coefficients in a commutative ring AAA. In other words, replace AAA with R\mathbb{R}R and A[[x]]A[ [x] ]A[[x]] with the ring C=C∞(R)C = C^\infty(\mathbb{R})C=C∞(R) of C∞C^\inftyC∞ functions on R\mathbb{R}R. (Doing it with polynomials would probably be equally convincing.)

So again we have the ring of dual numbers D=R[y]/(y2)D = \mathbb{R}[y]/(y^2)D=R[y]/(y2). Given a point x0∈Rx_0 \in \mathbb{R}x0​∈R, Hadamard's lemma allows us to expand any function f(x)∈Cf(x) \in Cf(x)∈C in the form f(x0)+a1(x−x0)+g(x)(x−x0)2f(x_0) + a_1(x - x_0) + g(x)(x - x_0)^2f(x0​)+a1​(x−x0​)+g(x)(x−x0​)2 for some unique number a1a_1a1​ and function g(x)∈Cg(x) \in Cg(x)∈C, and f′(x0)f'(x_0)f′(x0​) is according to standard definition this value a1a_1a1​. In other words, there is by this lemma a canonical isomorphism

C/(x−x0)2C≅DC/(x - x_0)^2C \cong DC/(x−x0​)2C≅D

which maps the residue class of f(x)f(x)f(x) to f(x0)+f′(x0)y∈Df(x_0) + f'(x_0)y \in Df(x0​)+f′(x0​)y∈D. In fact any homomorphism ϕ:C→D\phi: C \to Dϕ:C→D, written in the form ϕ(f)=ϕ0(f)+ϕ1(f)y\phi(f) = \phi_0(f) + \phi_1(f)yϕ(f)=ϕ0​(f)+ϕ1​(f)y, is given by (1) a homomorphism ϕ0:C→R\phi_0: C \to \mathbb{R}ϕ0​:C→R, with any such on C=C∞(R)C = C^\infty(\mathbb{R})C=C∞(R) being evaluation at a uniquely determined point x0x_0x0​, and (2) a derivation ϕ1:C→R\phi_1: C \to \mathbb{R}ϕ1​:C→R, meaning a linear function satisfying ϕ1(fg)=ϕ1(f)ϕ0(g)+ϕ0(f)ϕ1(g)=ϕ1(f)g(x0)+f(x0)ϕ1(g)\phi_1(f g) = \phi_1(f)\phi_0(g) + \phi_0(f)\phi_1(g) = \phi_1(f)g(x_0) + f(x_0)\phi_1(g)ϕ1​(fg)=ϕ1​(f)ϕ0​(g)+ϕ0​(f)ϕ1​(g)=ϕ1​(f)g(x0​)+f(x0​)ϕ1​(g). There is a whole tangent line’s worth of possible derivations, but the particular one we want will take the function f(x)=xf(x) = xf(x)=x to its correct derivative 111 at x0x_0x0​. Hence we would want the ϕ:C→D\phi: C \to Dϕ:C→D such that ϕ(x)=x0+1⋅y\phi(x) = x_0 + 1 \cdot yϕ(x)=x0​+1⋅y. Since CCC is the free C∞C^\inftyC∞ ring on a generator xxx, this condition uniquely determines ϕ\phiϕ (the book by Moerdijk and Reyes would be a good reference for the theory of C∞C^\inftyC∞ rings).

The set-up I used just packages all these ϕ\phiϕ into the single homomorphism δ:C→C⊗RD≅C[y]/(y2)\delta: C \to C \otimes_\mathbb{R} D \cong C[y]/(y^2)δ:C→C⊗R​D≅C[y]/(y2) that sends xxx to x+yx + yx+y, so that when we compute the composite

C→δC⊗RD→evx0⊗1R⊗RD≅DC \stackrel{\delta}{\to} C \otimes_\mathbb{R} D \stackrel{\mathrm{ev}_{x_0} \otimes 1}{\to} \mathbb{R} \otimes_\mathbb{R} D \cong DC→δC⊗R​D→evx0​​⊗1R⊗R​D≅D

we find that it sends f(x)f(x)f(x) to f(x0)+f′(x0)yf(x_0) + f'(x_0)yf(x0​)+f′(x0​)y, as promised.

I haven’t checked the nLab to see to what extent we’ve already attested to these facts, but it’s pretty standard material in SDG and algebraic geometry.
